name: Measuring for Baking
summary: Why a scale beats cups, how to measure flour when you only have cups, and a cups-to-grams chart that matches the recipes.

sections.heading: Why baking needs more care
blocks: A stew forgives an extra handful of anything. A cake doesn't: flour, fat, sugar, eggs and leavener work as a set of ratios, and if one drifts the texture changes. Too much flour is the most common problem, and it gives dry cookies, dense cakes and stiff dough.

A **kitchen scale** fixes most of it. A gram of flour is a gram however you scoop it, while a cup of flour can vary a lot from one person to the next. Weighing is also faster: put the bowl on the scale, press tare (zero), add the first ingredient, tare again, add the next.

sections.heading: Measuring flour with cups
blocks: No scale? Then how you fill the cup matters more than anything else.

items: Stir the flour in the bag or canister to loosen it.
Spoon it into a dry measuring cup until it's heaped over the top. Don't shake or tap the cup.
Sweep the excess off with the back of a knife.

blocks: Dipping the cup into the bag and scooping packs the flour down, so you get noticeably more of it than the recipe means. That's the usual reason a recipe comes out dry or tough the first time.

blocks.text: The recipes here are written for spooned-and-leveled flour, about 125 g per cup. Some sources use 120 g; either works, the difference is small.

items: **Brown sugar** is packed: press it into the cup firmly enough that it holds the cup's shape when you tip it out.
**Liquids** go in a clear liquid measuring cup on the counter. Read it at eye level, not from above.
**Sticky things** like honey, molasses and peanut butter slide out of a cup or spoon you've wiped with a little oil.
**Spoons** are level unless the recipe says heaping: fill, then sweep flat.
**Butter** sticks in the US are marked in tablespoons: one stick is ½ cup, 8 Tbsp or 113 g.

sections.heading: Cups to grams
blocks: Weights for one level US cup (237 ml), measured the way described above. These are the values the recipes' metric amounts use, so a recipe shown in metric and one shown in cups come out the same.

blocks.caption: Water and milk: 1 cup is 237 ml, which weighs about 240 g.

sections.heading: Small amounts
blocks: A household scale that reads in 1 g steps can't weigh half a teaspoon of baking soda accurately, so for small amounts spoons are often the better tool. Approximate weights of one level teaspoon:

rows: Table salt or fine sea salt

blocks.text: That salt table is why recipes say which salt they mean: a teaspoon of Diamond Crystal kosher salt is about half as salty as a teaspoon of table salt. In these recipes, plain "salt" means table or fine sea salt.
